extra.message: The `get_client_ip` function trusts the `X-Forwarded-For` header directly by taking its first value. An attacker can spoof their IP address by sending a crafted `X-Forwarded-For` header (e.g., `X-Forwarded-For: 8.8.8.8`). The comment acknowledges this is trusted to nginx, but the code itself doesn't validate the header source. This IP is used for audit logging and login event tracking.

The get_client_ip function trusts the first value in the X-Forwarded-For HTTP header as the client IP address. If the application is directly accessible (not behind a reverse proxy that strips or overwrites this header), an attacker can spoof their IP address by sending a crafted X-Forwarded-For header. This taints the IP address stored in LoginEvent records, AuditEvent records, and user.last_login_ip, compromising audit trail integrity.

The PasswordChangeView requires authentication but has no rate limiting. While authenticated, an attacker with a stolen session could attempt to brute-force the old password, or a logged-in user's session could be abused to change passwords repeatedly.

The PasswordResetView is used directly with no rate limiting. An attacker can submit unlimited password reset requests, causing email flooding to users and enabling email enumeration (by observing response differences between existing/non-existing emails).
The PasswordResetConfirmView (which accepts uidb64+token and sets a new password) has no rate limiting. An attacker could brute-force the reset token to hijack password reset flows.

The `AppLoginView` login handler has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism. An attacker can submit unlimited login attempts to brute-force user passwords. While `LoginEvent.recent_failures()` exists in the models to count recent failures, it is never called by the login view or any middleware to enforce throttling.

The login failure handler stores the `User-Agent` HTTP header directly into the database (truncated to 300 chars) without sanitization. While Django's ORM prevents SQL injection, unsanitized user agent values stored in the database and potentially displayed in the admin interface could enable log injection or stored XSS in admin panels.
The profile_view POST handler updates user profile data with no rate limiting. An attacker could submit unlimited profile updates, potentially causing database write exhaustion or abuse for storage.

The invite_accept view processes account creation via invite tokens with no rate limiting. An attacker who obtains a valid invite token (e.g., through email interception or token leakage) could rapidly create multiple accounts or brute-force tokens. Account creation endpoints are abuse-prone and should be throttled.

The invite token is passed as a URL path parameter (`/invite/<token>/`). This means the token can leak through HTTP Referer headers when the invite page loads external resources, through server access logs, browser history, and can be observed by anyone with access to the user's screen or network traffic. The token is a bearer credential that grants the ability to set a password for a customer contact account.

In the `invite_accept` view, when a `ContactInvite` token is presented for a contact that already has a linked `User` account (from a previous invite or seed), the code updates the existing user's password and full name (lines 126-129). If a new invite token is generated for a contact that already has a user account, anyone with that token can change the existing user's password and effectively hijack the account. The `used_at` check only prevents replay of the same invite, but doesn't verify that the contact doesn't already have an active user.

The full ContactInvite model object (including the secret `token` field) is passed to the template context in the invite_accept view. The ContactInvite model has a `token` field at models.py:167 which contains the one-time invite secret used to authenticate invite acceptance. Passing the entire model object to the template risks leaking the token if the template renders `{{ invite.token }}` or `{{ invite }}`. Even if the current template is safe, future template modifications could expose the token.

The `OrganizationForm` includes `owner` and `assigned_staff` as editable fields. While the form accepts a `requesting_user` parameter, it does not verify that the requesting user has authorization to change ownership or staff assignments. The authorization for these sensitive modifications must be enforced by the view, but the form itself provides no gate. If a view uses this form without proper authorization checks (e.g., an account manager editing their own org could promote themselves), it allows unauthorized organization takeover.

The `clean_target_url` method in WebhookForm blocks `localhost`, `127.*`, `192.168.*`, `10.*`, `169.254.*`, and `172.16-31.*` ranges, but does NOT block the hostname `0`. On many systems, `http://0/` resolves to `127.0.0.1` (localhost). This allows bypassing the SSRF protection and targeting localhost services.

The `AdminUserForm` exposes `role`, `is_staff`, `is_active`, and `primary_organization` as form fields. If any view uses this form without enforcing that only platform admins can access it, a lower-privilege user could escalate their privileges by changing their own role to `PLATFORM_ADMIN` or setting `is_staff=True`.

The seed_demo management command defines a hardcoded password DEMO_PASSWORD = 'Demo!Password123' (line 42) which is used for all demo user accounts (lines 383-395, 469) and customer portal users (lines 461-473). This password is printed to stdout at the end of the seeding process. While this is a seed script for demo data, the hardcoded credential still exists in production source code and could be exposed if the seed script is run in production or if the source code is leaked.

The Webhook model stores the webhook signing `secret` as a plaintext CharField with no encryption or hashing. The field declaration is `secret = models.CharField(max_length=80, default=secrets.token_urlsafe)`. While generation uses secure randomness (`secrets.token_urlsafe`), the secret value itself is persisted in cleartext in the database. A database compromise would expose all webhook signing secrets, allowing an attacker to forge webhook payloads that will pass signature verification on customer endpoints.

The `safe_break` template filter uses `mark_safe()` on unsanitized user input, marking the output as safe HTML without escaping any HTML/JavaScript. The filter only replaces newlines with `
` tags but does not escape HTML entities. Any template that renders user-controlled data (e.g., escalation comments, organization notes, document descriptions) through `{{ variable|safe_break }}` will output raw HTML, enabling stored XSS.

The `change_stage` view reads the deal object, checks the transition validity via `is_valid_deal_transition(deal.stage, new_stage)`, and then writes the new stage — all without a row-level lock (`select_for_update()`). Two concurrent requests reading the same starting stage could both pass the transition check, then both write different stages. The second write would overwrite the first, effectively skipping the intended state machine and allowing invalid transitions (e.g., LEAD directly to CLOSED_WON).

The `change_status` view reads the escalation object, checks the transition validity via `is_valid_escalation_transition(esc.status, new_status)`, and then writes the new status — all without a row-level lock (`select_for_update()`). Two concurrent requests reading the same starting status could both pass the transition check, then both write different statuses, allowing invalid state machine transitions.

Notification links are constructed using the escalation PK and formatted as raw strings. If the escalation title contains special characters, it could lead to issues in the notification display. However, the link itself is a fixed pattern, so the redirect risk is limited.

The `mark_read` view redirects users to the URL stored in `note.link`. This link is set by other application handlers (e.g., escalation replies, status changes) and if any of those handlers allow user-controlled content in the link, this becomes an open redirect.

When `ENABLE_REAL_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY` is enabled, the webhook's `target_url` is used directly in `urllib.request.Request()` and `urlopen()` without server-side re-validation. The URL was validated at creation time through `WebhookForm`, but the handler does not re-validate before making the actual HTTP request, creating an SSRF risk if the form validation is bypassed.

When `ENABLE_REAL_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY` is True, the `test_delivery` function makes an HTTP request to `hook.target_url` using `urllib.request.urlopen`. Although the WebhookForm validates URLs for loopback/RFC1918 at creation time, if the setting is enabled, it could be used for SSRF if a webhook URL was modified directly in the database.

The user_edit view processes POST requests to modify user details including roles. There is no rate limiting or throttling, allowing an attacker to brute-force role escalation or submit rapid changes.
The user_disable view processes POST requests to disable user accounts. There is no rate limiting, allowing rapid account disabling attacks.
The user_enable view processes POST requests to enable user accounts. No rate limiting is applied.
The API key creation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting. An attacker could flood the system with API keys, exhausting storage and operational capacity.
The API key rotation endpoint processes POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly rotate API keys, which could invalidate legitimate keys (DoS).
The API key revocation endpoint processes POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly revoke all API keys.
The contact creation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly create thousands of contacts.
The contact edit endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The contact invitation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly send large numbers of invitations.
The contact deletion endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The escalation reply endpoint in the customer portal accepts POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to flood escalations with replies.
The deal creation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The deal editing endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The deal stage change endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The deal deletion endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly delete all deals.
The document upload endpoint accepts POST requests with file uploads without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly upload large numbers of files.
The document metadata editing endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The document deletion endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly delete all documents.
The escalation creation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The escalation editing endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The escalation status change endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The escalation comment addition endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The CSV import endpoint accepts POST requests with file uploads and processes up to 5,000 rows. There is no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly import large amounts of data.
The notification mark-as-read endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The mark-all-notifications-as-read endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The organization creation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The organization editing endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The organization deletion endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting, allowing an attacker to rapidly delete organizations and all associated data.
The webhook creation endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The webhook editing endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.
The webhook deletion endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting.

The webhook test delivery endpoint accepts POST requests without rate limiting. When ENABLE_REAL_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY is True, this triggers actual HTTP requests to the webhook target URL. Without rate limiting, an attacker could rapidly trigger many outbound requests.
The 'packet_ref' GET parameter is concatenated with BASE_EXPORT_DIR without sanitization, allowing path traversal via '../' sequences.
The `packet_ref` GET parameter is directly concatenated into a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use '..' sequences to read arbitrary files outside the intended directory.

The `url` parameter is taken directly from user input and passed to `urllib.request.urlopen`. An attacker can make the server send requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts, bypassing firewalls and accessing internal services.

The `acct_delta_121` function accepts `amount` and `state` values from user input and directly modifies a financial ledger's balance and state. An attacker can set arbitrary amounts and state values, including potentially setting negative balances or approving unauthorized states.

The function reads `state` and `amount` directly from the client request body without any server-side validation. The attacker can set arbitrary ledger state (e.g., 'approved', 'rejected') and manipulate the balance.

In `acct_delta_121`, the `amount` is parsed directly from user-controlled request data (`payload.get("amount", request.GET.get("amount", "-250"))`) with NO positive check and NO upper bound. The operation `ledger["balance"] -= amount` means a negative amount increases the balance instead of decreasing it. The default amount is already -250, which adds 250 to the balance. An attacker can pass arbitrarily large negative amounts to inflate balance, or pass 0 for a free operation.
The `state` field from user input is directly assigned to the ledger object without validation or allowlisting. An attacker can set arbitrary state values.

In `acct_delta_121`, the ledger `state` field is assigned directly from user-controlled request data via `payload.get("state", request.GET.get("state", "approved"))`. An attacker can set the state to any value (e.g., `"approved"`, `"rejected"`, `"pending"`, or arbitrary strings), bypassing any intended state machine or approval workflow.
The `lane` parameter from user input is passed directly to Django's redirect() function without validation. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, enabling phishing attacks.

The `acct_workset_rebind_191` view parses the request body (JSON or POST) and calls `workset.update(payload)` — wholesale binding of all user-supplied fields onto a dict containing privileged attributes (`role`, `tier`, `approved`, `balance`). An attacker can set any of these fields to arbitrary values, including changing `role` to `admin`, setting `approved` to `True`, or setting `balance` to any amount.

The function reads a JSON payload from the request body and applies it directly to a workset dictionary via `workset.update(payload)`. The default workset has `role: viewer, tier: standard, approved: False`, but the attacker can overwrite these to `role: admin, tier: premium, approved: True`. No server-side validation is performed on the fields.
The `acct_workset_rebind_191` function merges user-supplied payload directly into a workset dictionary. An attacker can set arbitrary fields including `approved` to `True`, `role` to `admin`, etc.

User-controlled 'ref' GET parameter is used directly in a file path construction. An attacker can write arbitrary files by using '../' sequences. Additionally, SSN and credit card numbers from query parameters are written to disk in plaintext.

The `ref` GET parameter is used to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use '..' sequences to write files anywhere on the filesystem. Combined with the SSN/card data being written, this is a severe file write vulnerability.

Social Security Numbers ('ssn') and credit card numbers ('card') are accepted from query parameters and written to a file on the server filesystem in cleartext without encryption. The file path is also returned in the response.

SSN and credit card numbers are transmitted via HTTP GET query parameters (ssn=, card=). URL parameters are logged in server logs, browser history, and transmitted in cleartext over non-HTTPS connections.

The `acct_vault_stash_233` function writes user-supplied SSN and credit card numbers (`request.GET.get("ssn")`, `request.GET.get("card")`) to a file without any validation of format, length, or whether the values are appropriate for the operation. Combined with the path traversal from `request.GET.get("ref")`, an attacker can write arbitrary SSN/credit card data to files.
The endpoint uses MD5 hashing for digest generation. MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for security purposes.
The function uses MD5 to hash a user-supplied phrase. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.

MD5 is used for hashing user-supplied data. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. If this hash is used for security purposes (token verification, integrity checks), it could be bypassed.
MD5 is used for hashing user-supplied phrases. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.
The function uses MD5 (hashlib.md5) to hash user-provided data. MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for security purposes.
The `acct_identity_ping_333` function is missing the `_wrk_gate` authentication check that all other partner console endpoints use. Anyone can call this endpoint without any authentication.
Authentication verifier values ('4812', '5930') are hardcoded in the source code for the 'north' and 'south' handles. These are used as shared secrets to verify identity.

The endpoint returns different HTTP status codes and messages for 'unknown handle' (404) vs 'bad verifier' (403). This allows an attacker to enumerate valid account handles by observing the response difference.

The `acct_origin_mirror_369` function reflects the `Origin` header value directly into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests, bypassing the Same-Origin Policy.

The `Origin` header from the request is reflected in the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is set. This allows any website to make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint, leaking sensitive data.

The endpoint reflects the Origin header directly into Access-Control-Allow-Origin AND sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to this endpoint.

User-controlled 'fragment' GET parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection. Although _wrk_gate() provides token-based auth, token compromise or bypass makes this exploitable.

The `acct_jinja_cast_381` function takes a user-supplied `fragment` parameter and passes it directly to `jinja2.Template('Result: ' + fragment).render()`. This allows arbitrary Jinja2 template execution, which can lead to remote code execution through Jinja2's sandbox bypass.

The `name` GET parameter is user-controlled and used to construct a file path without sanitization. The request body is then written to that path. Path traversal sequences like `../` allow writing files anywhere the application has write access, potentially overwriting critical system files or application code.

The `acct_shell_probe_399` function takes a user-supplied `host` parameter from GET query string and passes it directly into `os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host)`. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands by including shell metacharacters (;, |, `, $(), etc.) in the host parameter.

User-controlled 'host' GET parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to os.system(). No sanitization or escaping is applied. Although _wrk_gate() provides token-based auth, if the token is ever compromised, leaked, or bypassed, this allows arbitrary command execution.
The endpoint uses random.choice() (Mersenne Twister PRNG) for generating alphanumeric codes instead of cryptographically secure randomness.

The `random.choice()` function from Python's standard `random` module is used to generate what appears to be a code/token. The `random` module uses Mersenne Twister, which is not cryptographically secure - its outputs are predictable if an attacker can observe a few values.
The function uses random.choice() (Mersenne Twister PRNG) to generate 'nonce' codes. This is not cryptographically secure and predictable if an attacker can observe previous outputs.

The `random.choice()` function from Python's `random` module is used to generate security-sensitive codes. The `random` module uses Mersenne Twister, which is predictable if an attacker can observe multiple outputs.
The `acct_frame_slip_419` function explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (disabling browser XSS filters) and sets an empty `Content-Security-Policy` header, removing clickjacking and XSS protections.
The endpoint explicitly sets X-XSS-Protection to 0 and sets Content-Security-Policy to an empty string, removing browser security protections.
The function explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (disabling browser XSS filters) and sets an empty `Content-Security-Policy` header. These security headers are being actively weakened.

SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled using `ssl._create_unverified_context()`. This allows man-in-the-middle attackers to intercept and modify the HTTPS request to the partner endpoint.
The `acct_badge_gate_439` function reveals sensitive payroll and casework details when provided with a badge value of 'lead'. This exposes sensitive operational data.

The function reads a privilege level (`ops_badge` with value `lead`) from a client-controlled cookie or header and uses it to grant elevated access. Any attacker can set the cookie `ops_badge=lead` or header `x-ops-badge: lead` to gain elevated privileges including payroll and casework access.
Authorization decisions are based on a client-controlled cookie or header value (`ops_badge`/`x-ops-badge`). An attacker can set this value to `lead` to gain elevated access.

The function parses user-supplied XML with an unsafe parser that allows DTD loading, entity resolution, and network access. An attacker can perform XXE attacks to read local files, perform SSRF, or cause denial of service (e.g., Billion Laughs attack).

The Django SECRET_KEY is set via environment variable with a hardcoded fallback: 'dev-secret-change-me-please-not-for-production'. If DJANGO_SECRET_KEY env var is not set (e.g., deployment misconfiguration), this predictable key is used. An attacker who knows the SECRET_KEY can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens, and any HMAC-signed data, leading to full account takeover.

The SECRET_KEY has a hardcoded fallback value 'dev-secret-change-me-please-not-for-production' if DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. If deployed to production without this env var, the secret key is publicly known, allowing attackers to forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and password reset tokens.

The DEBUG setting defaults to True: `DEBUG = _env_bool("DJANGO_DEBUG", default=True)`. If the DJANGO_DEBUG environment variable is not set in a production or staging deployment, Django will run in debug mode. This causes verbose error pages with full stack traces, local variables, settings values (including SECRET_KEY, database passwords, and API keys when they are added), source code snippets, and environment details to be displayed to any user when an error occurs. Furthermore, many security hardening measures (SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE, HSTS, SSL redirect) are only applied when DEBUG is False (lines 124-130), meaning they are all disabled in this scenario.

The DEBUG setting defaults to True via `_env_bool('DJANGO_DEBUG', default=True)`. If the DJANGO_DEBUG environment variable is not explicitly set to 'false' in production, the application runs in debug mode, which exposes detailed error pages with stack traces, settings (including SECRET_KEY, database passwords), and query information to end users.

The PostgreSQL database connection configuration does not include any TLS/SSL parameters (such as sslmode=require, ssl=True, or OPTIONS with SSL certificates). All data transmitted between the application server and the database — including queries and result sets containing PII and customer data — flows over an unencrypted TCP connection.

The database password defaults to 'crm_saas' if the DB_PASSWORD environment variable is not set. Combined with the default DB_USER='crm_saas' and DB_NAME='crm_saas', a deployment that does not set these environment variables will have a known database credential.

The database configuration has hardcoded default credentials (username 'crm_saas', password 'crm_saas') that are used if the respective environment variables are not set. If deployed without overriding these env vars, the production database uses well-known default credentials.

The database PASSWORD falls back to 'crm_saas' when the DB_PASSWORD environment variable is not set. This hardcoded default password is predictable and publicly visible in the source code. Any production deployment that fails to set DB_PASSWORD will use this weak default, allowing anyone with network access to the database to authenticate.

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are only set inside the 'if not DEBUG:' block (line 124). Since DEBUG defaults to True, if the env var is unset in production, session and CSRF cookies are transmitted over unencrypted HTTP without the Secure attribute, allowing network attackers to steal them.

CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY is set to False, meaning the CSRF token cookie is accessible to JavaScript via document.cookie. This exposes the CSRF token to any XSS vulnerability on the site, enabling cookie-based CSRF attacks.

Security-critical settings (SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS, SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS, SECURE_HSTS_PRELOAD) are all inside a 'if not DEBUG:' block. A misconfiguration that leaves DEBUG=True in production disables all HTTPS enforcement, HSTS, and SSL redirect protections.

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are only set to True when DEBUG=False. Since DEBUG defaults to True, session and CSRF cookies are transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, allowing session hijacking via network sniffing or man-in-the-middle attacks.

The urls.py imports partner_console and registers 20+ routes with obfuscated path names (ops/folio/acct-roster-card-001/, ops/shell/acct-probe-399/, etc.) that appear designed to hide endpoint purposes rather than enforce proper access control. The handler functions (in partner_console.py, not shown) may lack authentication/authorization.

The user's email (u.email) is rendered inside a JavaScript string in an onsubmit event handler: onsubmit="return confirm('Disable {{ u.email }}?');". Django's auto-escaping converts single quotes to ' in HTML context, but the browser's HTML parser decodes ' back to ' before passing the attribute value to JavaScript. This allows an attacker with a crafted email containing a single quote and JavaScript payload to break out of the string and execute arbitrary JavaScript when a staff user attempts to disable the user.
The escalation.customer_summary field is rendered with |safe_break in the customer portal template, allowing stored XSS against customer portal users who view this escalation.
Escalation comment body (c.body) is rendered with |safe_break in the customer portal template, allowing stored XSS against customer portal users viewing the conversation thread.

The deal.notes field is user-controlled content (set by staff via deal edit forms) that is rendered with the |safe_break filter, bypassing auto-escaping. This allows stored XSS in deal internal notes.

The escalation.customer_summary field is user-controlled content (set by staff via forms) that is rendered with the |safe_break filter. If this filter calls mark_safe() internally (as its name suggests), it bypasses Django's auto-escaping and allows stored XSS. An attacker with staff access can inject arbitrary JavaScript into escalation summaries that executes when any staff user views the escalation detail page.

The escalation.internal_summary field is user-controlled content (set by staff) that is rendered with the |safe_break filter, bypassing auto-escaping. This allows stored XSS through internal escalation notes.
Escalation comment body (c.body) is user-controlled content that is rendered with the |safe_break filter, bypassing auto-escaping. Comments can be posted by any authorized user, allowing stored XSS.

The org.website field is rendered inside an href attribute: href="{{ org.website }}". While Django auto-escapes HTML characters, it does not prevent javascript: protocol URIs. An attacker who can set the organization's website to 'javascript:...' creates a link that executes arbitrary JS in the viewer's browser.

The org.notes field is user-controlled content (set by staff via organization edit forms) that is rendered with the |safe_break filter, bypassing Django's auto-escaping. This allows stored XSS in organization internal notes.

The organization name (org.name) is rendered inside a JavaScript string in an onsubmit event handler: onsubmit="return confirm('Permanently delete {{ org.name }} and all its records?');". Django's HTML auto-escaping is insufficient for JavaScript string context because ' is decoded by the browser's HTML parser. An attacker who can set or modify the organization name can inject a JavaScript payload that executes when an admin attempts to delete the organization.

The template renders {{ field.help_text|safe }}, marking the help text as safe HTML without escaping. If any form field's help_text is populated from user-controllable data (e.g., dynamic form customization), this directly enables stored XSS. The safe filter bypasses Django's auto-escaping.

The template renders {{ field.help_text|safe }}, marking the help text as safe HTML without escaping. Same pattern as invite_accept.html — if help_text is dynamically populated from user input, this is stored XSS.
The template renders {{ field.help_text|safe }}, marking the help text as safe HTML without escaping. Same dangerous pattern as the other two auth templates.
